title: Makhana Kheer: A Creamy, Nutritious Dessert for Sawan Fasting Season
excerpt: This simple fox nut kheer combines roasted makhana, full-fat milk, and saffron into a satisfying vrat-friendly treat rich in protein and fiber.
body:
• Makhana kheer is a grain-free, satvik dessert ideal for Sawan Somwar fasts, made with ghee-roasted fox nuts simmered in full-fat milk.
  • Fox nuts pack roughly 9.7 grams of protein and 14.5 grams of fiber per 100 grams while containing almost no fat, providing sustained energy during fasting.
  • The kheer takes about 30–40 minutes, requires only seven core ingredients, and can be served warm or chilled.
  • Sawan 2026 runs from July 30 to August 28, with Somwar vrats falling on August 3, 10, 17, and 24.

Why Makhana Kheer Belongs on Your Sawan Table

With Sawan 2026 now underway — the holy month of Shravan runs from July 30 through August 28 this year according to the North Indian Purnimant calendar — millions of devotees are observing Monday fasts dedicated to Lord Shiva. That means grain-free, satvik meals are in high demand, and few desserts fit the bill as neatly as makhana kheer.

Makhana, also called fox nuts or popped lotus seeds, has been a staple of Indian fasting cuisine for centuries. The puffed seeds of the Euryale ferox plant are naturally gluten-free, low in fat (just 0.1 grams per 100 grams), and surprisingly rich in protein and fiber, according to Healthline. When slow-cooked in milk with saffron and cardamom, they soften into a creamy, pudding-like dessert that satisfies without weighing you down.

Ingredients You Will Need

This recipe serves four and comes together with pantry staples found at any Indian grocery store:

  • 1 cup makhana (fox nuts)
  • 1 litre full-fat milk
  • 1 tablespoon ghee
  • ¼ cup sugar or jaggery (adjust to taste)
  • ½ teaspoon cardamom powder
  • 6–8 strands of saffron, soaked in 1 tablespoon warm milk
  • 2 tablespoons each chopped almonds, cashews, and raisins

Step-by-Step Method

1. Roast the makhana. Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan on low flame. Add the fox nuts and roast for 5–7 minutes, stirring frequently, until they turn crisp and lightly golden. You should be able to snap one between your fingers. Remove from heat and let them cool briefly, according to The Daily Jagran.

2. Crush a portion. Take about a third of the roasted makhana and crush it into a coarse powder using a rolling pin or a quick pulse in a blender. This acts as a natural thickener, giving the kheer its signature creamy body without any added starch, a technique recommended by the recipe site Mahakatha.

3. Boil and simmer the milk. In a separate heavy-bottomed pan, bring the milk to a gentle boil on medium heat. Stir frequently to prevent it from sticking to the bottom.

4. Add the makhana. Stir in both the whole roasted fox nuts and the crushed powder. Reduce the heat to low and simmer for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the makhana softens and the milk begins to thicken.

5. Sweeten and flavour. Add sugar and stir until dissolved. If using jaggery instead, turn off the flame first to prevent the milk from curdling — a tip highlighted by Cadbury Desserts Corner. Stir in cardamom powder, saffron milk, and chopped nuts. Cook for another 3–5 minutes.

6. Rest and serve. Remove from heat, cover, and let the kheer rest for 5 minutes. The makhana will continue absorbing flavour. Serve warm as prasad or chill in the refrigerator for a refreshing summer treat. It keeps well for two to three days.

Nutritional Profile and Fasting Benefits

Makhana punches above its weight nutritionally. Per 100 grams of raw fox nuts, expect roughly 347 calories, 9.7 grams of protein, 14.5 grams of dietary fiber, and 76.9 grams of carbohydrates, according to nutritional data compiled by NutriScan. The seeds also deliver 210 milligrams of magnesium and 60 milligrams of calcium per 100-gram serving.

Combined with full-fat milk, the kheer provides a sustained release of energy — exactly what devotees need during daylong Somwar fasts. The low glycemic index of makhana helps keep blood sugar stable, making this dessert practical as well as devotional.

Tips From the Experts

Roasting is the make-or-break step. Under-roasted makhana turns soggy in the milk rather than soft and fluffy. Full-fat milk is non-negotiable for richness; low-fat versions will not reduce into the same creamy consistency. And if the finished kheer thickens too much as it cools — a common occurrence — simply stir in a splash of warm milk before serving.

For Diaspora Kitchens

Makhana is now widely stocked at Indian grocery stores across North America, the UK, and the Gulf. Online retailers have expanded availability further. For those observing Sawan away from home, this kheer is one of the simplest ways to keep fasting traditions alive. The entire recipe takes under 40 minutes, and the ingredients are pantry-friendly enough to whip up on a weeknight Monday evening after work.
